Athamas, son of Aeolus, brother of Cretheus, as Apollonius himself says (III 560) 'for both Cretheus and Athamas were sons of Aeolus', has two children by Nephele, Phrixus and Helle. When she died, he married a second wife, Ino. She, as a stepmother, plotted against the children from the previous wife, and by roasting the seeds she gave them to the farmers for sowing. They sowed them in the

earth, but the earth, having received them, did not produce the annual crops because they had been roasted and thus sown. Then Athamas, gathering the seers as king, asks them the cause, wishing to learn it. She sends to them, promising to give many gifts, so that they would say that unless the children of Nephele, the former wife of Athamas, were first killed, the earth would not produce crops. Persuaded, the seers say these things, having returned to Athamas. When the children of Nephele, Phrixus and Helle, were about to be killed, a ram came down. Then taking them on its back, it goes into the sea and thus begins to swim. Coming to the Trojan sea, it throws off Helle, whence from her the Hellespont was named, and carries Phrixus to Scythia. There he slaughters the ram and sacrifices it to Zeus Phyxios, because he escaped the plot of his stepmother; he marries Chalciope, daughter of Aeetes, king of the Scythians, and has by her four children, Argus, Cytisorus, Melas, Phrontis, and thus dies there.
